props.title: Follow the Fleet
props.initialSlug: Sailors, singers & romance light up the dance floor

sections.content: Follow the Fleet (1936) exemplifies the pinnacle of Fred Astaire and Ginger Rogers' collaborative magic during RKO's golden age of musicals. Irving Berlin's score powers this nautical romance, marking their fifth pairing after Top Hat (1935). The film cleverly adapts the stage musical "Shore Leave," transforming it into a showcase for Astaire's Navy sailor and Rogers' dance hall performer. Director Mark Sandrich, who helmed several of their best collaborations, brings a breezy efficiency to the proceedings while maximizing the impact of the dance numbers, particularly in the show-stopping "Let's Face the Music and Dance" sequence.

sections.content: The film's production values reflect RKO's commitment to the Astaire-Rogers formula, with lavish Art Deco sets by Van Nest Polglase creating a gleaming backdrop for Berlin's memorable songs. Harriet Hilliard (later famous as Harriet Nelson) makes her film debut here, adding a parallel romantic subplot that enriches the main story. The naval setting distinguishes it from other entries in the series, though it maintains the signature mix of comedy, romance, and spectacular dance numbers that defined the duo's partnership.

What sets Follow the Fleet apart is its grittier, more working-class atmosphere compared to the high-society settings of Top Hat (1935) and The Gay Divorcee (1934). The dance hall sequences presage similar settings in later classics like On the Town (1949) and Sweet Charity (1969). Berlin's score includes "Let Yourself Go" and "I'm Putting All My Eggs in One Basket," showcasing both the romantic and comedic sides of the Astaire-Rogers partnership. sections.content: Follow the Fleet represents a crucial bridge between early sound musicals like 42nd Street (1933) and the more integrated story musicals that would follow in the 1940s and 1950s. Its influence can be traced through later naval-themed musicals like Anchors Aweigh (1945) and South Pacific (1958), while its working-class elements anticipate the grittier realism that would eventually emerge in films like West Side Story (1961).
